links.reason: The shared figure is real (திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண் டற்று / அரவு சேர்ந்த திங்கள்), but it is a stock eclipse simile used for different things; 'a flexible figure' is only the shared image. The gains clauses invent a 'lawful guarded display' contrast and a 'ready sign' that neither text states.

Not incompatible claims: Nedunalvadai shows the king sleepless at night (பள்ளி கொள்ளான்) visiting wounds, 2353 shows Civakan charging the uncle with the wounded (புண்கொண்டு போற்றிப் புறஞ்செய்க) and resting. A scene contrast is not a tension, and the claimed historical drift from presence to command is not in either text.

Kural 327 forbids killing another even at the cost of one's own life; 249 says kings who kill to keep the body long (கொலையினான் முயன்று வாழும்) last only a few days (சிலபகல்) and sink in rebirth (பிறவி முந்நீர் அழுந்துவர்). The verse adds a reason (brief body, worse rebirth) the couplet lacks.

Verse 9 gives the king's fault (காமம் கனைந்து கன்றி, சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and 25 only summarises Civakan's killing of the enemy (பகை நாம் அறக் கொன்ற வாறும்) in the same patikam; this is plot sequence, and 25's line 4 is uncertain about who is the spear-bearer. 'Frame the whole plot' overstates.
links.text_issue: Verse 25 line 4 (நஞ்சு ஊறும் வேலான்) is ambiguous between Civakan and the enemy

links.reason: The matched punishment is real: 1932 செம்பினில் பொங்கனற் பாவைகள் புல்லப் புணர்ப்பார், 2769 செப்புப் பாவை யாதகா தென்னப் புல்லி. But it is a common Jain hell trope in two verses of the same school, and the pair teaches little beyond the difference in starting point.

Both are Paranar poems naming Nannan, but 292 mentions only a green fruit (புனல்தரு பசுங்காய்) and 73 only the mango felled (நறுமா கொன்று); that they are two halves of one tale (fruit, then tree) comes from tradition, not the Tamil, and no poem refers to the other.

Both list a minister's qualities (குடியோம்பல்/குடிகாத்தல், வன்கண்மை/வன்கண், நூல்வன்மை/கற்றறிதல்) and Elathi adds more, but the correspondence is of idea more than of 'near-identical words', and Elathi's lines 2-4 are read doubtfully; the pair is a list comparison.
links.text_issue: Site text lacks line 1 of Elathi 17, the line the link rests on; lines 3-4 doubtful

links.reason: 1880 only describes the king's insignia (குடையின் நீழலான், கவரி வீச) and has no claim; the 'height from which he will walk away by choice' is imported from later plot. Naladiyar 3 (வினைஉலப்ப வேறாகி வீழ்வர்) is a warning the verse does not answer or limit, so QUALIFIES does not fit.

1706 shows a conception omen (மதியம் வாய் அடைந்தது); it does not say pleasure bears fruit in a longed-for son or answer Naladiyar 54's claim that the wise see pain in pleasure (இன்பம் இடைதெரிந் தின்னாமை நோக்கி). The qualification is read into the verse.

980 is a narrator's picture of a youth's charms capturing a girl's eyes (கன்னி கண்களைச் சிறைகொண்டிட்டான்); it states no view that the pull is natural or good. Tirumanthiram 204 warns men off smiling women (முலைநலங் கொண்டு முறுவல்செய் வார்மேல்). A scene against a warning, with no incompatible claim, is not a tension.

The shared figure is real: ஆக்கை உள்ளுறை ஆவி / யாக்கை நாடி and bird seeking the nest (சேக்கை நாடி ... புள்), against Kural 338 குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழியப் புள்பறந் தற்றே. But the verse does not limit the couplet, and K338 is not about a shell that 'feels nothing'; that the epic 'reworks' it is asserted, not shown.

282 prophesies that the arriving youth will wed the king's daughter and rule the earth with the complete wheel (நிறைந்த நேமி இந்நிலமும் ஆளுவன்); 290 shows the hero set on ruling by the wheel (நேமி ஆளவே) given the wheel and the nine treasures (நேமி தான்முதல் நிதிகள் ஒன்பதும்). A prophecy and its fulfilment. Indra's grace is from the next verse, not these.

Adjacent verses in story order. 1350 has the spear-bearer pierced and falling (சுடர்வேலான்), 1351 has the golden-banner king fall and the army break; the note treats these as two falls but they are probably one man, and 'the champion's body the army's footing' is the note's gloss.

The verse does not say the king crowned his sons first: it says he becomes a muni (மாமுனி ஆகி நிற்ப) and the sons leave the land's burden on a minister (பெருநிலப் பாரம் வைத்து), which hardly shows duty fulfilled. The 'late step after duty' premise of the qualification is not in the Tamil.

2010 asks equanimity to abuse, praise and neglect (வையினும் வாழ்த்தினும் வாளா விருப்பினும்); Kural 151 praises forbearance with scorners. These are different virtues (inner evenness, forbearance), and the couplet makes no claim to be the whole of calm, so 'covers only half' is not what it says.

The couplet names apportioning (வகுத்தல்) among a king's skills; 207 only lists towns given away, to Vayantakan and unnamed others. Nothing says the recipients risked themselves in captivity, or that this is 'the last duty of rule'. It is an illustration of the rule.
Real sequel of a king laying down the sword (வாளும் மாற்றி) and later asking pardon (முன்பு செய்த சிறுமைகள் பொறுக்க); but 311 has no 'taking his own refuge', and the arc is largely plot order.

Both use the fruit image (காமத்துக் காழில் கனி; கனியும் கருக்காயும்). But 1191 says nothing about wishing quarrels away; it speaks of requited love. 1306 adds that love without quarrels is imperfect, so it qualifies rather than contradicts it.

314 shows the deity taking the shape of the maid Sanbagamalai (கூனியது உருவம் கொண்டு ஓர் தெய்வதம் குறுகிற்று), the scene behind 10's தெய்வம் துணையாய்த் துயர் தீர்த்த வாறும். The summary's help is shown to come through disguise as a familiar servant.

Adjacent verses in sequence: 1104 gifts to the fire-priests, 1105 the learned chief priest gets a rain of wealth. 'Wealth follows the Veda, not the families' is the note's inference; 1105 only says the skilled priest received.

319 is Vijayai's lament (நல்வினை செய்து இலாதேன்); 343 is a stock dawn simile (அல்லல் வெவ்வினை போல அகன்றதே) about the travellers' night, with no reference to her. A simile in the narrator's mouth does not contradict her self-blame.

690 is Tivittan's defiant message (முறையுள தெனினது முயன்று கொள்கவே); 695 is the minister's reply, a conjured trick (மாயங் காட்டி உளைவித்து) to drive him into the lion. The later verse answers the challenge.

Both likenesses are stock: 1233 sets cloud against cloud and sea against sea, 17 has the host கடலென. 'A source for the sea-army figure' implies dependence the texts do not show, and 'unopposed host meets its match' is not in Pur 17.

Both bathe a royal bride with water from jewelled pots borne on elephants (யானை ... மணிக்குடம்; களிற்றின் உச்சி ... குடத்தில்), a real shared detail. But it is a conventional wedding rite, and 'marks Lakkanai's wedding as in the line of the contest bride's' is only interpretive. 2431's ஏற்றி is ambiguous.

Both hold the tiger that will not eat prey fallen on its side (Nal 300 இடம்வீழ்ந்தது உண்ணாது; Pur 190 இடம்பட வீழ்ந்தென ... உண்ணாதாகி) as a mark of high-mindedness, one for honour against heaven, the other for choosing friends. The exact refusal is shared and each book turns it differently.

354 says the king, hearing of the elephant's rebirth, sees the kingdom and its pleasures will not last (நில்லல) and calls his son; it does not show him giving up throne, wives and lands 'within a verse'. The pair is a story illustrating a rule (நின்றன நில்லா), with no cost or limit added.

The note says Vimalai's horoscope 'names the sign he will give', but 1976 only says the astrologers wrote her fortune (எழுதி இட்டார்) and its next lines are obscure. The 'king's place, merchant's goods' contrast rests on an unreadable verse.

274 tells that the ascetic was lord of Kalinga who ruled the whole land alone (முழுதாண்ட சிங்கம்); 276 has him give up lands, women, army (நாடுநகரங்களும் ... அகல்க). Story order, with the second answering the first only loosely.

There is no shared image: 1467 has a list of what fails (வலியும் ... வனப்பும் கடைபோகா) and no figure, while K332's figure is the dance-hall crowd. They share the theme of fading wealth, so the type is wrong.

Nal 33 gives the response to the ripened fruit (தொல்லைய தென்றுணர்); 2762 gives the sowing and eating of deeds (வித்தி ... உண்ணும்). A real complement, but both are the same common Jain karma doctrine and the pair adds little the doctrine does not.
The same simile appears (1137 மடுபுலி கண்ட மான்; 2196 புலிகாண் கலையிற் புலம்பி), but it is a stock one. That Kattiyangaran sent the men of 1137, and the tie to 2197, are not in the two verses.

Both say present fortune is the fruit of earlier deeds (வினையதனின் விளைவு; முன்பவர் செய்கையினாலே). But 1839's 'way' (நெறி) is unspecified, so reading it as giving imposes Tirumanthiram's content; the gains clauses are illustrative, not true gains.

Both mention circling the Jina's feet (வலஞ்செய்து; வலங்கொண்டார்), but 2560 is a declaration at worship, not a 'boast' or 'pride', and 3017's speaker is an unnamed hymn voice whose lines are hard. The note reads psychology into both.
The four wives of 241 are not named in the Tamil (நால்வரும்); the names come from the note. Adding Virisikai to three queens is plot arithmetic, not an answer or reversal.

Both address bees about a woman's hair and teeth (குவளை ... கூந்தலுள் ... வண்டுகாள் ... எயிறு; Kur 2 கூந்தலின் நறியவும் உளவோ ... செறியெயிற் றரிவை). The similarity is striking, but the address to bees is a common topos, and 'learned borrowing' is not demonstrable.

Soolamani 301 praises two ministers as masters of treatise and omen-books, and says nothing of native wit. That is silence, not a claim limiting K636 (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு). The 'different weighing of counsellor' is invented.

Marusi adds an appraisal (யான் பல மன்னர் ... கண்டனன் அன்ன நீர்மையார் அரசர் இல்லை) of a king; the verse does not show it differs from his message or is untrue, and K688 speaks of faithful relay (வாய்மை வழியுரைப்பான்), not of judging kings. The 'stretch of truthfulness' is not in either text.

The deed matches K327's subject (killing another to save oneself, வாழ்வதோர் உபாயம் நாடி ... போழ்படப் பிளந்து), but the narrator only reports it and the city mourns; 'fear of the king' and the sceptre's pressure are not in 1163. An illustration, with the chapter tie as invention.

Pur 184's காய்நெல் அறுத்துக் கவளங் கொளினே and யானை புக்க புலம் is the same figure as 2907's காய்த்த நெற் கவளம் தீற்றின் ... களிறு கழனி மேயின், used again for a king's measured taking. The epic reuses the Sangam image, with a king advising his successor.

Both say deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord, but 1549's line 4 is hard and the marker's reading uncertain. Reading K5's unnamed இறைவன் as the Jina is one sectarian reading, and the epic is not shown to read the Kural.
511 already names the lord (பிண்டி நாதன் நாண்மலர்ப் பாதம்), so 2812 does not newly 'name whose feet'. Both are Jina praise from different speakers; the pair is a recurring motif.

181 praises him who conquered the harsh dust of karma (வெம்மைசெய் வினைத்துகள் விளிய வென்றவன்) but does not say praise stops deeds clinging; identifying K5's இறைவன் with that Jina is the note's reading, and the gains clauses are circular.

Two eclipse figures in one chapter (2308 திங்கள்போல் அரவினால் கொள்ளப்பட்ட; 2324 பருதி ... நாகம் வாய் போழ்ந்து), a real contrast of caught and freed. But in 2308 he is blowing the conch in rage, not under threat, so 'moon in the grip in the thick of the fight' misreads the simile and 'brighter' is gloss.
